content: How can you get featured by Kenyan influencers and media? Most pitches fail for the same reason: they describe the product. A journalist or creator is looking for something their audience will care about. Your product is only the proof. Start with the creator side. Odipo Dev estimates Kenyan creators earned about Ksh 1.07 billion from brand work in 2025, and says small and medium businesses make up roughly 80% of that market. Beauty and personal care drew the most brand attention, with 174 active companies. It is an estimate, and HapaKenya's summary doesn't explain the method, but the direction is clear: creators are used to working with small shops, and the busy ones get many offers. So give them a reason to say yes. Three story angles a shop can own: 1. A problem you solve that customers talk about. Imagine a Nairobi skincare shop that stocks products tested on darker skin. That is a story. "20% off serum" is not. 2. Something you know that others don't: what sells in your area, what customers return and why. 3. A real change: a new branch, a delivery area you now cover, a local supplier you switched to. For media, Vincent Owino, a business reporter at The EastAfrican, keeps it plain: ask whether your story interests that outlet's readers, send it by email rather than phone or WhatsApp unless you already know the journalist, and check print schedules so it arrives well before the deadline. It's the real risk of AI-written code: not speed, but false confidence. Early in this project my tests were green, and an audit still found dozens of issues. So I built the answer into the process: 🛡️ Every change is reviewed by a separate AI agent whose only job is to reject it until it sees proof. 🛡️ Architecture rules are enforced automatically. If code breaks them, it doesn't build. 🛡️ I chose Rust because its compiler catches mistakes before they ever reach production. content: Visit my website 3d My #1 building philosophy is something I picked up in YC. I was kind of skeptical of it at first, but it carried us through 3 pivots and $52M in funding. I think for a long time I kind of subscribed to the perfection thing. Like why would you put something out into the world that isn’t perfect yet? YC changed my mind. When we were in YC we had to pitch an imperfect product. Actually we weren’t even pitching a product, we were just pitching an idea. So before we’d built anything, much less perfected anything, we were already getting people interested. That was the first time it clicked for me. The first version of what we created was totally imperfect. But we wouldn’t have known how to make it better if we didn’t have feedback. Then we completely changed our product from Glimpse 1.0 to Glimpse 2.0 and we wouldn’t have been able to do that if we didn’t know the market. People get stuck perfecting the right product and the right TAM and the perfect ICP. But the thing is, until you put all of that stuff out into the world you actually don’t know what is or isn’t right and what does or doesn’t work. Similar rules apply to building product. When we’re building out our product and addressing client requests, wherever it’s possible to get out an MVP and get it into the hands of a customer to iterate with, we do it. content: A late post, but I wanted to share it anyway. In September I spent three days at WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America in San José, which bills itself as the world’s largest developer event. "Can AI write code?" already feels like an old debate. Then it was AI agents. Now anyone can code, and the question in every room was harder: how do we make it secure? We have entered the era of governance. AWS showcased Strands Agents, their open-source Python SDK, where you give an agent a model, a goal and tools and it works out the rest. The more an agent decides on its own, the more control you need over what it can touch. That idea ran through the panel “There’s No Such Thing as Vibe Strategy, Vibe Security, or Vibe Scale,” with PwC leaders. AI gets you to a prototype on vibes, but production still takes strategy, security and discipline. Anyone who reviews code sees this, and research confirms it: a Stanford study found developers using AI assistants wrote less secure code while feeling more confident in it. An amazing session by Sheilah K on “Agents That Own Their Inference” made a sharp point: per-token fees work for a prototype, but at production scale the unit economics break. In my understanding  with AI prices falling so fast, companies can’t compete on price alone. content: A company might think it sells a product. Its customers might be buying something completely different. A hotel sells rooms. But its customers might be looking for peace of mind, convenience or simply a stay without any hassles. A coffee shop sells coffee. But people might keep coming back for the familiar routine, the atmosphere or just having a place they enjoy spending time in. And a jewellery brand sells gold, diamonds and design. But a customer might be buying a memory, celebrating a milestone or choosing something to pass down to the next generation. The product is the same. The reason for buying it can be very different. I find this one of the most interesting parts of marketing. Businesses tend to focus on what they make, the features they offer and the price they charge. But customers don’t always think that way. They think about what the product means to them, how it fits into their lives or what it helps them achieve. And I think this difference matters more than businesses sometimes realise. If you focus only on the product, it’s easy to end up competing on features and price. But when you understand why people buy, you start seeing other ways to connect with them. content: If we can conjure anything with AI, do we still need PMs? I hear this more and more. My answer: more than ever, but the job looks less like taking orders and more like curating. Think about a gallery. Most of its collection sits in the archive. For each exhibition, the curator picks a handful of pieces that belong together and tell one story. (PMs have an archive too. We call it the backlog.) For years, building was the bottleneck, so a PM's job was mostly moving requirements along. Now AI makes building close to free. When building isn't the bottleneck, deciding what to build is. Elon Musk has a five-step "Algorithm" for building things (it's in Walter Isaacson's biography of him): 1. Question every requirement 2. Delete 3. Simplify and optimize 4. Accelerate 5. Automate AI helps a lot with steps 3 to 5. Steps 1 and 2 are still a human job, and they're exactly the curator's job. Skip them, and AI just helps you optimize the wrong thing faster than ever. Now imagine the gallery can suddenly afford every artwork in the world. Hang them all and nobody can follow the story. Every piece still needs looking after, too. Features are the same: building got cheaper, maintaining didn't. My favorite example is Whoop. Feature for feature, it loses to the Apple Watch by a mile: no screen, no notifications, and it can't even tell you the time. When accounting records contain unresolved discrepancies or uninvestigated timing differences, executive decisions are built on guesswork. Across growing businesses and CPA firms in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, UAE, and Kuwait, unreliable reports usually stem from three core areas: Surface-Level Bank Reconciliations: Clearing transactions is not enough. Unexplained variances, uncleared checks, and carried-forward adjustments must be investigated immediately. Payment Gateway Disconnects: E-commerce and multi-channel platforms (Stripe, PayPal, Shopify, Amazon) carry refunds, processing fees, chargebacks, and reserve holds. Logging gross receipts without reconciling processor payouts distorts real margins. Neglected Balance Sheets: A clean P&L means little if clearing accounts, accruals, prepayments, and intercompany loans are left unreviewed. content: Beveiligingsincident bij Nvidia Brev: mogelijk blootgestelde SSH-sleutels Nvidia heeft maatregelen genomen na een beveiligingsincident op zijn Brev-cloudplatform. Bij het incident was gedurende een periode van 16 dagen ongeautoriseerde activiteit zichtbaar. Daarbij kunnen SSH-sleutels die worden gebruikt om toegang te krijgen tot virtuele machines van klanten zijn blootgesteld. Volgens Nvidia vond de verdachte activiteit plaats tussen 4 en 20 oktober. Het bedrijf heeft de betrokken SSH-sleutels inmiddels vervangen en de betreffende klantomgevingen voorzien van nieuwe sleutels. Nvidia zegt geen bewijs te hebben gevonden dat de mogelijk buitgemaakte gegevens daadwerkelijk zijn misbruikt. Onduidelijk blijft hoe de aanvallers toegang tot het platform kregen en of klantgegevens of workloads zijn ingezien. Juist dat maakt een incident met SSH-sleutels relevant. Wanneer een aanvaller over een geldige private sleutel beschikt, kan die sleutel afhankelijk van de ingestelde rechten en aanvullende beveiligingsmaatregelen toegang geven tot servers of cloudomgevingen. Het incident staat niet op zichzelf. AI-ontwikkelplatforms en cloudinfrastructuur vormen een steeds aantrekkelijker doelwit omdat daar waardevolle credentials, API-sleutels, environment variables en toegang tot krachtige compute-infrastructuur samenkomen. content: Visit my website 1h Attackers tested stolen AI keys within 30 minutes. Could you rotate yours that fast? Wiz's "Black October" report counts at least nine AI developer platforms that disclosed security incidents in a single month, from Fireworks AI and Railway to Warp and, on 30 October, Northflank. Wiz found no single shared vulnerability. The common thread was the target: stored environment variables, especially the ones holding AI provider keys. The numbers are worth sitting with. In two cases of downstream abuse Wiz tracked, attackers made a validation call within 30 minutes of the credential access, then ran roughly 800k and 1.7M Amazon Bedrock calls. Wiz estimates more than $100k in usage at list price. 😳 The advice was blunt: treat every environment variable as decrypted and rotate everything. The lesson most teams miss: your PaaS control plane is part of your secrets perimeter. A key stored in a vendor's dashboard is only as safe as that vendor's worst day. What I'd check this week: → Inventory every third-party platform holding your secrets. Most teams undercount this badly. → Replace static cloud keys with short-lived credentials (OIDC federation, IAM roles) wherever the platform supports it. → Scope AI keys tightly: one per workload, limited to the models and regions you actually use, with quotas and spend alerts set. → Run a rotation drill. headline: Pharmacy Business Adviser Independent Pharmacies Australia IPA QLD
content: Technology, trust and the mental load of diabetes. 💙 95% Time in Range over the last 24 hours. I’m incredibly thankful for diabetes technology, particularly my MiniMed insulin pump, which has been a genuine game changer for me. Before transitioning from multiple daily injections (MDI) to insulin pump therapy, I was already achieving similar Time in Range results, often sitting in the high 80s to 90%. But what those numbers didn’t show was the mental workload behind achieving them. Managing insulin, anticipating glucose changes, making decisions throughout the day and trying to balance all of that alongside a demanding job was becoming exhausting. Recognising that early burnout was important. Transitioning to my MiniMed pump hasn’t removed the work involved in managing diabetes, and technology certainly isn’t something we can simply set and forget. The data we put in, the decisions we make and the work we continue to do still matter. But having technology that I can increasingly trust has helped alleviate some of that mental burden and made a meaningful difference to how I feel, function and perform throughout my day. Diabetes has so many hidden variables that can affect how we think, work and operate. Often, those challenges aren’t visible to the people around us. For me, having the right technology has helped make navigating those invisible challenges a little easier. And sometimes, that’s what a genuine game changer looks like. content: “Prediction of Future Combined Sewer Overflows: Case Study of San Francisco” Combined sewer overflows, untreated stormwater, and sewage discharging into water bodies are expected to get worse under a rapidly intensifying hydroclimate. As storms grow more intense and potentially larger, sea level rise, coupled with groundwater level rise, will likely reduce the effective drainage capacity of many existing stormwater systems. A recent study compared a hydrologic-hydraulic model (PCSWMM) and a hybrid mass balance method for estimating combined sewer overflow (CSO) volumes to San Francisco's Eastside combined sewer systems.  A mass-balance approach was used only as a screening tool, NOT as a replacement for the calibrated hydraulic model. In managing wastewater and stormwater through 29 outfalls into San Francisco Bay, the model's validation showed good agreement (e.g., Nash-Sutcliffe 0.65–0.75; square error <3.0). While individual outfalls may vary, the overall system estimates were deemed reliable. Monthly CSO predictions ranged from within 1% to four times the values observed, with better accuracy over multi-year periods, deemed suitable for long-term planning. Future climatic scenarios for 2030–2035 and 2090–2095 considered base rainfall, sea level rise, and groundwater levels.  Saltwater inflows due to sea level rise could increase CSOs by up to 9.8%. I was pleased to deliver a lecture on Dispute Resolution in Civil Engineering to final-year civil engineering students at @Manipal Institute of Technology, as part of their Contract Management elective. On a construction site, technical competence is essential. Engineers also need to understand contractual obligations, document instructions, recognise variations, issue timely notices and manage payment issues. A technically sound decision can still have costly contractual consequences. author: Ahmed Alhassan
headline: PROJECT CONTROLS MANAGER | SR. MASTER PLANNING LEADER Specialized in Oil & Gas & Giga-Projects | PMP®, PMI-SP® | PMI Global Awards Judge
content: The Recovery Schedule Fantasy Compressing remaining durations on Primavera P6 without adding resources or changing logic isn't a 'Recovery Plan'. It's just a mathematical lie to keep the client happy. When a mega EPC project falls 20% behind schedule, panic sets in. The immediate executive order to the PMO is always the same: "We need a Recovery Schedule by Monday." Here is what usually happens next: Instead of changing the physical execution strategy, we change the math. We go into Primavera P6 and simply reduce the durations of the remaining activities. We crush a 30-day activity into 15 days. We squeeze a 60-day procurement cycle into 45 days. The software recalculates. The end date magically aligns with the contract. The client is happy, the executives are relieved, and the new baseline is approved. But the site team knows the truth: The plan is completely impossible. The Reality of Recovery: You cannot recover time with software. You recover time with resources. If you are going to compress a duration in P6, you must attach a real-world constraint to it: * Are we adding a night shift? * Are we changing the logic to allow concurrent work? * Are we bringing in more heavy equipment? If the answer is no, then you haven't built a Recovery Plan. You’ve just built a fantasy to delay the inevitable argument. A mature Project Controls team refuses to submit a mathematical lie. content: with Jasper Zhang, Ph.D. • 10h • Edited New research from Blu Putnam, Hyperbolic's Senior Research Analyst and former Chief Economist of CME Group, on why GPU rental indices don't agree, and what that means for GPU compute futures. The market for buying, selling, and renting advanced GPU compute time is expanding rapidly. There are hyperscalers and neoclouds. There are frontier AI developers, and startup firms building specialized AI agentic tools. There is an active secondary market linking users that reserved more GPU compute time than they need with other users seeking short-term on-demand GPU compute time. The next stage involves the launch of GPU compute futures contracts. The GPU compute space is likely to be quite active and become its own asset class. To track GPU hourly compute rental costs, indices are being created. If the new futures contracts are to be cash settled, they require a reliable, reproducible, publicly available reference index for GPU hourly rental costs. Herein lies the complexity. There are important differences in definitions and methodologies among the current index providers. The challenges are immense when trying to create indices in a highly fragmented and nuanced marketplace. There are different GPU compute chips. New chips coming online can impact the rental costs of older chips. Different locations, from global to US only, variable power costs, and the connectivity of data centers can matter, too. content: Before approving a ₹12 lakh budget for native Android and iOS apps, ask one question: Which customer requirement genuinely needs native technology? I’ve seen too many Indian founders treat app development as a status symbol: "We need our logo on the Play Store." Here is what happens in reality: A potential customer clicks your ad. Instead of experiencing your product, they hit a 100MB download barrier, app store permissions, installation delays, and an onboarding wall. When a PWA is the Smarter Choice: ▪️ Direct Web Distribution: Users access your product instantly with zero download lag. ▪️ Unified Codebase: One clean React/Next.js codebase serves Web, Mobile, and Desktop. ▪️ Sub-Second Loading: Service workers cache core UI assets for instant, reliable repeat visits. ▪️ Push Notifications: Full Web Push support across modern Android and iOS (16.4+). ▪️ Ideal For: E-commerce stores, B2B SaaS, booking platforms, and CRM dashboards. 2. For me, the best part was finally meeting face to face with people we work with every day by email and phone. Those conversations are a big part of why this event matters so much to our industry. A few things stay with me: Capacity and turnaround times are still the big challenge. Almost every conversation came back to getting aircraft back in service faster, and that starts with responsive engineering support that never cuts corners on airworthiness. Parts availability is a constant pressure. With supply chains still stretched, operators need partners who can source the right parts quickly, with full traceability and the right documentation. Digital tools are no longer optional. Operators want software built around real engineering and maintenance workflows, turning aircraft data into faster, better-informed decisions on the hangar floor. At Ziegler Aerospace, these are the problems we work on every day, across engineering services, aircraft parts procurement and software engineering for aviation digital tools. Our vision is simple: to be the partner that keeps aircraft flying safely, efficiently and sustainably. What we can do for you: ✅ Reduce aircraft downtime with fast, reliable engineering and technical support for airlines and MROs ✅ Supply the aircraft parts you need quickly,

It draws on the 2026 Sikich U.S. Internal Audit Priorities Survey, which shows that AI is now routine in audit work: 90% of internal audit functions use it, and 77% include AI assessments in their audit plans. In 2022, only 3% of leaders saw AI and automation as an emerging risk. In 2026, that figure is 35%. The article’s central point is that adoption is no longer the main issue. The question is whether assurance is keeping pace with AI’s spread across the organisation. It highlights five priorities for auditors: 1. Know where AI is already in use. A complete inventory should include AI embedded in vendor software, features activated through routine updates and tools employees adopt on their own. 2. Prioritise AI risk by impact. Tier use cases by business impact, data sensitivity and the consequences of an inaccurate output, so assurance focuses where it matters most. 3. Go beyond governance and security. Governance alone does not show whether a system performs as intended. Among respondents auditing AI, only 53% review operational effectiveness, 40% address ethical use and bias, and 36% include model validation. 4. Test the controls, not just the policy. content: My framework of choice (primate.run) is great for vibe coding but I would not recommend it to everyone: That sounds like a contradiction, so here is the full picture. Primate is a universal web framework. I did not write it, I get nothing for saying this, and I still reach for it on most AI builds. What actually works: 1) Routes and views live in separate folders, and that stays obvious after an agent has written 40 files. In Next.js the client and server line blurs. Primate's file map does the explaining for me so my agent is never confused. 2) I can use a json database to start until I'm sure of my database schema and then graduate to a proper database (usually postgres). 3) It works like lego blocks. A backend route can be TypeScript alongside another one in Go. Frontend views can be React alongside a Svelte view. The runtime can be Bun, Node or Deno. Swapping a block is cheap. Great for quick projects where you want to figure out what you want to use. 4) It's insanely fast and has a crazy small amount of dependencies Now the part that makes me hesitate to use it on real production builds: A) The ecosystem around it is young. You have to manually add certain libraries and can't use their native cli, like shadcn for instance. headline: Agentic AI @ Ema | Building your universal AI employee  Ex-Rippling/Sharechat/Cashfree/Headout
content: I have seen people work with AI in two different ways. The first are people working in their own stream. A salesperson can judge a good pitch from a bad one. A product manager knows whether a PRD is good or bad. Experience is the filter. The second are people doing something they haven't done before. A non-technical founder building a tech product, or an engineer writing their first sales pitch. They have no filter yet, so the usual advice, write better prompts, misses the problem. You can't fix output you can't judge. What works when you're in the second group: 1. Start from what exists. GitHub is where developers share their work, and people have published skills and agents there built on the best research out there. 2. State the objective, not the task. Stop writing "do this for me", "give me this information", "write that". Since you have become a builder now, you need to understand the objective, and tell AI what it is. 3. Ask for explanations, not solutions. If you're writing a PRD, ask: What is the breaking part here? What is good about it? What is bad about it? Ask for the case for and the case against. You don't need to understand code. You just need to understand, in natural language, what something is going to do. AI can produce the work. Judging it is your job, and judgment is going to be everything in the future. … more 5 ​ ​ ​

content: A founder came to me with a 47-feature product spec and £80,000 in budget ready to build. He had 12 months of runway, zero active users, and was preparing to build the entire scope. His reasoning was familiar. Build everything first, then hope the market finds something in there worth paying for. That instinct is common among non-technical founders, but it is also the fastest way to burn an entire pre-seed round. When you hire an agency to build 47 unvalidated features, you commit your capital to assumptions. Development agencies are incentivized to scope large projects, write tickets, and bill for delivery. They build what is specified, regardless of whether anyone will pay for it. In practice, unvalidated features quickly become dead roadmap weight. Users either ignore them or get lost in the extra clutter. By the time you discover what actually solves a problem, you have spent your £80,000 and run out of runway to iterate. I convinced him to pause the agency contract and run a three-step validation alternative instead: 1. Identify the single feature that proves someone will pay. We reviewed the entire product spec and asked which single feature on its own proves someone will pay. We isolated that core loop and cut the remaining 46 features from v1. 2. Build only that core loop in 6 weeks for £14,000. Instead of locking into a long build cycle for £80,000, we scoped a tight build focused strictly on that one validated interaction. author: Adi Behlulovic
headline: Serial Entrepreneur and Technical Leader | CEO @ ScaleUp
content: AI will f*ck up your product. Here are a few ways I have seen it happen while working with startups over the last couple of years. #1 - You are unprepared for AI. Would you give someone unrestricted access to your credit card? Of course not. Yet people let AI loose on their entire codebase with no context, documentation or guardrails. You need boundaries. You need documentation. You need to give AI enough context to understand what it should and should not do. Otherwise, you basically handed someone the keys to your product without explaining how to drive. #2 - You never prioritized that roadmap. AI makes building fast. Really fast. And suddenly you are like a kid in a chocolate store without parents. 'Build EVERYTHING!!' Well, no. Shipping 20 more features does not automatically make customers happier. Simplicity > complexity. AI makes prioritization more important, not less. Talk to customers. Ask them what actually matters. Use MoSCoW, 100-point allocation, whatever the hell you want. Just stop guessing. Build gradually. Then ask if it actually made the product better. #3 - You gave too much to AI. The code these models generate today can be amazing. But AI is still... a tool. It does not magically understand your architecture, security requirements or which shortcuts will haunt you six months from now. Have a senior engineer navigate it. - Architecture. - Security. - Code review. - Tradeoffs. - Quality. Unless you are building a quick-and-dirty MVP. Then sure. Go wild. #4

content: We've never shipped software faster. But are we still engineering it better? AI-assisted coding has fundamentally changed software development. Features that once took a sprint can now be built in an afternoon. MVPs can go live in days. Development velocity has increased significantly. But there's a growing question we shouldn't ignore: Are we building software faster than we can understand, maintain, and own it? This is the hidden risk of vibe coding. When developers rely heavily on AI-generated code without fully understanding the implementation, the immediate productivity gains can create long-term engineering challenges. For SaaS businesses, this is particularly important. Shipping a product is only the beginning. The real challenge is continuously evolving it as customer needs, business rules, integrations, and compliance requirements change. Three areas are particularly at risk: 1. Maintainability Code that nobody fully understands becomes harder to debug, extend, and improve. 2. Engineering Ownership "The AI generated it" cannot be an acceptable answer during a production incident. 3. Change Confidence When engineers lack confidence in the codebase, even small changes become risky and expensive. There is also a longer-term concern: if AI reduces opportunities for junior engineers to learn through hands-on development, who will build the experience needed to maintain increasingly complex systems tomorrow? content: "Where do we put AI in this process?" is the wrong question. The right one is: "If we started today, with AI, would this process exist at all?" 👇 Automating = the same old steps, run faster by a machine. Redesigning = asking why those steps exist in the first place. When I led Telefónica's AI Factory, we saw this clearly in customer care. The first instinct was always: "add a bot that answers what agents already answer with a never ending PROMT." The real value came from a different question: What would have to happen for the customer not to need to call? From there, everything changes: the entry point, the decision rules, who steps in and when. 𝟰 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗜 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 1️⃣ Start with the business KPI, not the task. Fewer calls = lower cost. Faster resolution = more revenue. 2️⃣ Split the work again between people and agents. AI handles volume. People handle exceptions, judgment and relationships. 3️⃣ Build control in from day one. Traceability, human oversight where it matters, EU AI Act, GDPR. In a regulated industry, this can't be bolted on at the end. 4️⃣ Measure that KPI, not automation rates. A 100% automated process that doesn't improve the customer or the P&L is not a success. ➕ And the one rarely in the plan: change how teams work. Same work + new tool = nothing redesigned. For international readers, Tsinghua University plays a role somewhat comparable to MIT and Carnegie Mellon in the US, bringing together robotics research, engineering talent, startup networks and investors. Its robotics labs, alumni networks and startup ecosystem have created a strong concentration effect. Researchers become founders, former labmates build teams, and successful startups attract more talent and capital. According to IT Juzi, 75 out of 425 Chinese embodied AI startups have at least one founder with a Tsinghua University background. But what interests me even more is Galbot's approach to commercialization. At China's 2026 Spring Festival Gala, Galbot demonstrated impressive dexterous manipulation, including rotating two walnuts inside a robotic hand. Yet in actual retail stores and pharmacies, its robots mainly use wheeled bases and relatively simple grippers. Why? Because picking medicine from shelves doesn't necessarily require human-like legs or five fingers. It requires reliable perception, grasping and order fulfillment. AI made writing code faster. It didn’t eliminate the need to think. Someone still needs to review architecture, security, performance, business logic, and integrations. Someone needs to figure out whether the feature should even exist. And there’s still technical debt, which somehow never makes it onto the “urgent, needed yesterday” list. 😁 If every hour saved with AI is immediately filled with more tickets, you might end up with a team that produces code at an incredible speed. It’ll belong to companies that know how to use the time they’ve saved to make better decisions. Fewer pointless features. Better architecture. Faster experiments. Less rework. Picture the message nobody on an engineering team wants to receive: “Why did our dashboard stop updating?” Nobody on the team knew the dashboard existed. Someone outside engineering built it with an AI app builder. It reads production data with a full-access database key. It's deployed on a personal hosting account. And the person who built it has already left. This isn't a hypothetical problem. Engineers have been sharing versions of this exact story across the industry. The usual response? Ban AI tools for everyone outside engineering. I don't think that's the answer. People were running critical business processes on spreadsheets, macros, and scripts long before AI. The difference is that today's tools make it dramatically easier to build something that connects directly to production. So the real question isn't: “Who is allowed to build?” It's: “Can we list every app touching our production data and do we know who owns each one?” If the answer is no, start here: 1. Keep a simple inventory. Every internal app. What data it touches. Where it runs. Who owns it. 2. Stop handing out full-access credentials. Use scoped, read-only access wherever possible. A bug shouldn't be able to write, delete, or alter production data. 3. Use company accounts. An internal app shouldn't disappear with someone's personal hosting account when they leave. 4. content: My framework of choice (primate.run) is great for vibe coding but I would not recommend it to everyone: That sounds like a contradiction, so here is the full picture. Primate is a universal web framework. I did not write it, I get nothing for saying this, and I still reach for it on most AI builds. What actually works: 1) Routes and views live in separate folders, and that stays obvious after an agent has written 40 files. In Next.js the client and server line blurs. Primate's file map does the explaining for me so my agent is never confused. 2) I can use a json database to start until I'm sure of my database schema and then graduate to a proper database (usually postgres). 3) It works like lego blocks. A backend route can be TypeScript alongside another one in Go. Frontend views can be React alongside a Svelte view. The runtime can be Bun, Node or Deno. Swapping a block is cheap. Great for quick projects where you want to figure out what you want to use. 4) It's insanely fast and has a crazy small amount of dependencies Now the part that makes me hesitate to use it on real production builds: A) The ecosystem around it is young. You have to manually add certain libraries and can't use their native cli, like shadcn for instance. content: View my newsletter 20h The piece sets out three AI risk areas for companies under Chinese law (data and confidentiality, IP in AI outputs, algorithmic accountability) and recommends a compliance framework of data governance, vendor checks, human review and ethics oversight. A few quick questions before I draft: A recent article on corporate AI use under Chinese law sets out three areas of legal risk. The first is confidentiality, where staff upload business documents to public AI tools and some providers keep the right to use those inputs for training. The second is intellectual property, as AI output may not be protected, may reproduce someone else's work, or may carry open-source licence obligations in the code. The third is accountability for what the AI actually does, such as charging different customers different prices based on their personal information. The authors recommend a compliance framework covering data governance, vendor due diligence, human oversight and internal ethics review. It's sensible advice, and although the statutes differ, most of these risks would be familiar to anyone advising a business in Singapore. Where I think organisations tend to struggle is the gap between the framework and the working day. Most companies I come across have some form of AI policy by now. author: Michael Roberts
headline: CISSP CEH CHFI
content: Binance lost about $6.3 billion from a hot wallet, and the first cause it named was one compromised laptop. TRM says most of it crossed ten blockchains in about 20 minutes. No SOC wins that race. My position: when the gap between authorization and loss is shorter than your alert triage, detection becomes a postmortem tool. The control that counts is what a single endpoint can authorize on its own. Mid-market shops do not run hot wallets. You do run admin laptops holding Global Admin sessions, cloud CLI keys, CI/CD tokens and RMM consoles. Same shape. One machine, standing authority, no second human in the path. What is confirmed so far is thin. Co-CEO Richard Teng cited a compromised laptop. Later review found more breach points Binance has not detailed. The malware was built to destroy its own evidence. TRM and Chainalysis attribute it to TraderTraitor, the group tied to the 2025 Bybit theft, which also started on a developer machine. There, signers approved a transaction their own screens misrepresented. Root cause beyond that is not public. Anyone claiming certainty this week is guessing. Exposure check, on your five most privileged laptops: - ~/.aws/credentials holding long-term keys that start with AKIA - Token caches: ~/.azure/msal_token_cache.*, ~/.kube/config, ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml, ~/.npmrc - Entra sign-ins by privileged roles from devices not marked compliant - GitHub.com and GitLab personal access tokens with no expiry I recommend this order if one of those laptop

author: Peter Guerra

content: Latest #Cyber and #AI thoughts What happened: A tampered copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension sat on Cursor's marketplace for about 11 hours. Cleaning up after something like this is a race against scope, and AI can help CISOs win it, as long as humans keep control of the decisions. On October 29, malicious versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 of the Claude Code VS Code extension were available from about 2:27am to 1:35pm PT. Cursor says Anthropic did not write them, and Anthropic says its official channels were not affected. The package collected host and user details, tried to plant an attacker SSH key, opened a reverse tunnel, and set up persistence. On most macOS and Windows hosts the tunnel step failed without admin rights, but standard-user machines could still have had their host profile sent out and the SSH key planted. Why it matters: a trusted vendor name on an official marketplace was enough to run code with developer privileges, which put source code, cloud credentials, and CI access in reach. Your AI tools are now part of your software supply chain. How a CISO can use AI to remediate: Scope exposure in hours, not days. Use AI to correlate EDR telemetry, extension install logs, and marketplace records against the install window and the affected versions. Have analysts review the queries and results before anyone acts on them. Triage at volume. Key takeaways: - Never store passwords in plaintext. - Avoid weak or outdated algorithms such as MD5 and SHA-1. - Use secure password hashing algorithms like Argon2, bcrypt, or scrypt. - Never implement your own cryptographic algorithms. 🔹 2. A05 – Injection What happens when an application trusts user input too much? That's where injection vulnerabilities come into play. I explored concepts involving: - SQL Injection - Command Injection - Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) Security lesson: Never blindly trust user input. Use parameterized queries, proper input validation, and safe APIs. 🔹 3. content: Thiago Santos de Moura, Selma Güler and Yannic Noller at Ruhr-Universität Bochum tested something I've wanted someone to measure properly. What happens when an attacker writes the CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md file that a coding agent loads at the start of every session? Their paper, Security Impact of Coding Agent's Memory Files, plants a malicious project memory file in 36 SecRepoBench tasks (real C and C++ repositories, 12 CWE classes). Each file dresses up the removal of defensive checks as ordinary engineering guidance. Internal code should trust its caller, validation belongs at the boundary, that kind of thing. The files never say "security" or "attack" and never name a CWE. One version recommends, the other insists. They ran Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5 and OpenCode with Qwen 3.8 27B and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, then checked every completion against the original OSS-Fuzz proof of concept and the developer unit tests. The headline result is close to null. Secure completion rates moved between minus 8 and plus 6 percentage points, with no consistent direction. Underneath, 30 of 204 paired completions differed in security, 15 favoring the baseline and 15 favoring the poisoned run. With one run per task that can't be told apart from noise, and the authors say so plainly. The second question is where it gets uncomfortable. content: QS path in the next 5 years - 2031 From traditional MEP measurement to engineering cost optimisation. Traditional QS asks: How much cable, ductwork, piping and equipment are required? Future-focused QS asks: Why is this equipment required? Is its capacity justified? Can we achieve the same performance with a better engineering solution? What is its total cost over 20 years? The objective is to reduce unnecessary capital expenditure, improve energy efficiency, protect safety and deliver long-term value to the client. Strongest advice: Do not make Electrical and HVAC QS teams responsible only for reducing BOQ rates. content: 🏗️ Rebar Spacing: A Critical Factor in Reinforced Concrete Structural Safety Proper Reinforcement Detailing Ensures Concrete Quality, Structural Strength, and Long-Term Durability. In reinforced concrete construction, proper rebar spacing is not just a detailing requirement—it is essential for structural performance and construction quality. Excessive reinforcement congestion, particularly in beam-column joints, can prevent concrete from flowing and compacting properly, resulting in honeycombing, voids, poor bond, and potential durability issues. Key Engineering Considerations: 🔹 Control Reinforcement Congestion: Maintain adequate clear spacing between reinforcement bars to facilitate concrete placement. 🔹 Ensure Proper Concrete Flow: Allow sufficient space for concrete and aggregate to pass through the reinforcement cage. 🔹 Achieve Effective Compaction: Ensure proper vibrator access to minimize air pockets and honeycombing. 🔹 Follow Approved Drawings: Comply with structural drawings, reinforcement detailing requirements, and applicable design codes. 🔹 Protect Structural Durability: Proper concrete cover, compaction, and reinforcement detailing help protect steel against corrosion. Remember: A well-detailed reinforcement cage leads to better concrete placement, improved construction quality, and greater long-term structural reliability.
